messages.subject: Methods for grouping species for pooled detection function
messages.subject_clean: Methods for grouping species for pooled detection function
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm working on estimating bird abundances from a dry forest in Peru, using line transect distance sampling, I have 20 species – of course some are more commonly recorded (c.1000 records) and others rarer (<200 records). My aim is to have density estimates by species by site (26 sites) over my study area.

I'm looking to combine species into groups sharing similar detectability so that I can use a pooled detection function for the less common species. The idea would be to have some more common species plus rarer species in each group, but this will depend on the outcome of my grouping.

As I understand it, to group species, they need to have similar detection functions, this could be approximated by charactersistics of detection such as maximum observed distance, as used by Alldredge et al 2007. I have considered using such characteristics influencing detectability – maybe getting several metrics and using a cluster analysis to find likely groups. But then I was thinking – why not use a test to compare distance distributions directly eg Anderson-Darling two sample, or Cramér–von Mises test (with emphasis on distances closer to 0) to compare the shape of the detection fall-off across species. Each pair of species would have a test statistic – and these pairwise ‘distance’ values (lower the statistic, the more similar  the distributions) could be fed into a cluster analysis to create the groups.

I'm also considering using covariates but would like to try this separately first, and then maybe compare approaches, or combine them.
I'd be interested to hear any opinions about potential problems in using this method. Apologies if this is not clear , please let me know.

Thanks for any guidance

------------------------------------

messages.body_plain:
Christian:

About combining species for generating pooled detection functions.  I suspect the covariate approach is the one to use; it would allow you to "borrow strength" across species.  It is true you could do something like a K-S test of the respective detection histograms or more exotically conduct a cluster analysis.  However, place these analyses into some context:  you are doing an analysis (whether to combine) in anticipation of an analysis (detection function fitting) to produce an estimate of abundance.  I would suspect you will be looking for a more direct route to getting your analyses completed.

As an aside, you are trying to produce 520 density estimates for each species X site combination.  That will be quite an achievement by itself.  I suspect you will be challenged to have sufficient data for all of your combinations.  If you do need to pool data across species, recognise the species-specific estimates will not be independent because they share common data.  You will need to take care if you wish to make comparisons between estimates that are not independent.  Consult section 3.6.5 of Buckland et al. (2001).

Dear all,

I want to report average probabilities of detection for different subsets of the population based upon MCDS models, and can see two different approaches, which yield different results, and I’m trying to choose between them.

First just calculate the mean of the fitted p values for that subset of the population:

>ddf.result<-ddf(method=ddf.method,dsmodel=dsmodel,data=ddf.dat,  meta.data=ddf.meta.data)

> average.p<- mean(ddf.result$fitted[selected])

When all data are selected, this gives the same result as:

> mean(ddf.result$fitted)

[1] 0.5348632

My models assume clusters are independently detected,and cluster size is one of the covariates. Using this approach, I calculate probabilities of detection for individuals rather than clusters by weighting each cluster by its size when calcluating the mean.

Second (derived from the code for mrds:::plot.ds),  fit a detection function model for that subset of the population, and calculate the average.p values accordingly

    pdot <- ddf.result$fitted[selected]

  inverse.pdot.sum<-sum(1/pdot)

  ddfobj <- ddf.result$ds$aux$ddfobj

  m<- nrow(ddfobj$xmat[selected, ])

  n<-length(distance)

  p<-rep(0,n)

  for (i in 1:n)

  {

    x<-rep(distance[i],m)

    detfct.values <- mrds:::detfct(x, ddfobj,select = selected, width = width)

    p[i]<-sum(detfct.values/pdot)/inverse.pdot.sum

  }

  average.p <-mean(p)

When all data are selected this gives the same result as:

> summary(ddf.result)$average.p

[1] 0.4890873

This approach yields estimates of the average probabilities of detection for each subset of the population which correspond to the fitted curves returned by mrds:::plot.ds.

I don’t see how to calculate probabilities of detection for individuals using this approach.

The two approaches give similar, but different answers, and I’m just wandering exactly what the differences represent, and if one approach is to be preferred over the other.

Thanks for any help

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm attempting to obtain density estimates by site and by species, for a line transect design with terrestrial birds in north Peru, as mentioned on my previous post. For some species-site combinations, the sample sizes are quite small, so, as pointed out by Eric Rexstad, one recommended way to make the most of the data is to use covariates in the distance model.

If I have two levels of stratification (species, sites), then I think there are two possibilities for analysing the data, pooling all records for a particular site (using data filter to select one site), and using species as a covariate, or pooling records for one species across all sites, and using site as a covariate (data filter to select one species). First, I'd appreciate any thoughts on whether this is a sensible way to consider the analysis, and whether one method is more appropriate than the other. Would it depend on whether I thought that species characteristics (eg vocalisations, behaviour) had more influence on detectability (therefore use site as covariate) rather than site characteristics (habitat type, structure)? Also, would there be any way of selecting a best model between the two? I don't see how I can compare AIC values from Distance if using different data filters.

I've been doing some preliminary analyses with my data, and have found that I don't always get models converging. I've tried to build up the number of covariate levels gradually, and using one key function with a low number of adjustments, (eg I'm pooling all records for a particular site, and then used species as a covariate), in this case, I added species one at a time as covariate levels with the data filter, and obtained OK looking models until hitting one or two problem species with a small number of records at that site. Are there any guidelines as to minimum sample sizes per covariate when using the multi covariate method? In some cases, there are about 10 records per site.

Of course, ideally, more records would be obtained, but for rare species, and with limited resources for field work, I think it's interesting to try to find the best methods to get decent density estimates.

I appreciate any thoughts,

best wishes,
Christian

messages.body_plain:
Christian, sorry, I didn't read your earlier posting, but on the face of it, you don't need to decide between species and site.  You can pool all data, and use both species and site as factor-type covariates.  Thus for a rare species, you use data across all sites.  But do you really need site as a factor?  Do you have covariates recorded for each site or line relating to e.g. habitat?  If so, you might model site variability in detectability by including (continuous or factor-type) covariates relating to habitat, rather than by having a level for each site of a factor.  You can post-stratify by species or site to get your abundance estimates.  In the estimate tab of model defn, you need to check both the global and stratum boxes for both density and detection function.

Steve Buckland

I also attach the R file as well as the data we are using. Positions fo sightings and segments were derived from geographic coordinates using the latlong2km code.

As you may see from the plots coming from R, the segments are drawn following a wierd pattern, like connecting points that must be apart in the flight order. I tried to solve this getting the data in the flight order and nothing changed.

Any help is appreciated

Christian:

It is possible to produce site and species-specific detection probabilities when both are covariates in the detection function.  The detection probabilities would be used to adjust counts for imperfect detectability to produce the site/species specific estimates you seek.  However Distance does not directly report those estimates for you.  Similarly Distance will only produce abundance or density estimates at levels of study area, stratum (however defined) or sample.

It would require writing some bespoke code to make the pieces fit together.  Possibly some other subscribers to the forum have suggestions.

The code assumes that the observations are ordered (object x observer 1, object x observer 2, object y observer 1, object y observer 2 etc or (object x observer 1, object y observer 1, object x observer 2, object y observer 2 etc) and objects 895 and 894 are intermingled with other objects for the 2 observers which is causing the code to issue an erroneous message. When I reordered the records and ran your model it threw an error that you used a factor with only one level - which was seat because it only had one value for observer==1. The distance sampling detection function is for the pooled observations - seen by at least one observer.  You can use seat and expert in the mrmodel.  Observer type measures for the distance sampling detection function can only be done in pairs (ie a pair of experts vs a pair of non-experts) because the pairs of data are treated as a unit in the distance sampling detection function.

Hi Stewart and list,

mrds does expect an "observer" column in the data. The "partially
matched" warning means that R means that you have some other column in
your data with a title that starts "observer" and R has partially
matched the name (this is an R feature, so you can write "data$longvar"
and get the contents of "data$longvariablenamethatidontwanttotype").

So, in your case you might still have the wrong data in your model
(though if the results are close, perhaps not). It's safest to create
that extra column of all 1s to ensure that mrds is interpreting the data
as single observer.

Hope this helps.

best,
--dave
